sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Deccan Ulcer**: Aurangzeb's 27-year long stay in the Deccan (1681-1707) drained the imperial treasury and exhausted the Mughal army. 
• **Annexation Policy**: Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) to eliminate potential allies of the Marathas, which inadvertently removed the buffer states. 
• **Maratha Resistance**: Transitioned from 'Ganim-kava' (guerrilla warfare) under Shivaji to a war of attrition under Rajaram and Tarabai. 
• **Key Metric**: The collapse of the 'Jagirdari System' due to the scarcity of 'Paibaqi' (vacant land) in the Deccan.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix

Mains: Turning point from centralized to decentralized resistance.

Taxation systems (1/4th and 1/10th of revenue) used by Marathas to extract resources from Mughal territories.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Mughal Strategy**: 'Divide and Rule' by inducing Maratha Deshmukhs to defect. 
• **Maratha Strategy**: 'War of Independence' led by the Maratha nobility after the fall of Raigad.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Financial bankruptcy of the Mughal state and the rise of 'Zamidari' rebellions. 
• **Solutions**: Shift from centralized imperial control to decentralized regional confederacies.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'B-G-S' (Bijapur, Golconda, Sambhaji). 
• **Decoded Meaning**: The sequence of Aurangzeb's major Deccan focus: Bijapur (1686), Golconda (1687), and the capture of Sambhaji (1689).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the Treaty of Purandar (1665) with the later Treaty of Purandar (1776) during the First Anglo-Maratha War.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Imperial Overstretch' to describe Aurangzeb's Deccan policy in the context of Paul Kennedy's theory.

keyTakeaways: The Deccan campaign was the primary catalyst for the economic and military decline of the Mughal Empire.
The destruction of the Deccan Sultanates removed the 'buffer' that kept the Marathas in check.
Maratha resistance evolved from a personality-driven movement to a nationalistic struggle for 'Swarajya'.
